An Electric Banquet
Rochester Democrat and Chronicle
December 6th, 1896
Page number(s):
3
Buffalo Will Celebrate the Transmission of Electric Power.
Buffalo, N. Y., Dec. 5. — A banquet is to be given here at an early date by the Cataract Power and Conduit Company to celebrate the accomplishment of the scheme to utilize Niagara Falls electric power for commercial purposes in this city. The details are not yet decided upon, nor is the date fixed, but enough is known to show that it will be an historic event. The list of guests will take the name of the greatest and most distinguished men of the country. Among those who will be invited and who it is expected will attend are:
President Cleveland, Vice-President Stevenson, President-elect McKinley, Vice-President-elect Hobart, Governor Morton, Governor Binck, Mayor Strong, the governors of several states, the mayors of the principal cities, Thomas A. Edison, Nikola Tesla, and other celebrated electricians and men who have became famous in the sciences and the arts.
One thing that bothers the projectors of the enterprise is that the number of guests must be confined to 250 at the most. It is proposed to give the banquet at the Ellicott Club in Ellicott Square, which has the largest banquet hall in the city, and the seating capacity is limited to the number named.

Pittsburg. Feb. 27.(AP) — Lester J. Hendershot, 29 year old West Elizabeth, Pa., Inventor, whose fuelless motor has gained the interest of Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and others prominent in the aviation world, wants the "humbug" eliminated from reports on his invention, which he developed while experimenting on an effort to produce an improved compass.
"Make it clear to the world," he said, in commenting on stories giving various descriptions to his creation, "that radio and its allied phenomena have nothing to do with my motor.

Gloversville Daily Leader
February 13th, 1894
The February "Century" contains an article by Mr. T. C. Martin, editor of the "Electrical Engineer," on the work of the Serbian-American electrician, Nikola Tesla. The writer says:
"Mr. Tesla has advanced the opinion, and sustained it by brilliant experiments, of startling beauty and grandeur, that light and heat are produced by electrostatic forces acting between charged molecules or atoms. Perfecting a generator that would give him currents of several thousand alternations per second, and inventing his disruptive discharge coil, he has created electrostatic conditions that have already modified not a few of the accepted notions about electricity.
It has been supposed that ordinary currents of one or two thousand volts' potential would surely kill, but Mr. Tesla has been seen receiving through his hands currents at a potential of more than 200,000 volts, vibrating a million times per second, and manifesting themselves in dazzling streams of light. This is not a mere tour de force , but illustrates the principle that while currents of lower frequency destroy life, these are harmless. New York Herald
January 15th, 1899
Result, New Lease of Life
How This Tremendous Force Is To Be Generated Has Not Yet Been Revealed
No Insulator For Patients
Even Consumption, It Is Asserted, Will Be Routed by the New Discovery
Nikola Tesla, whose boldness in conceiving astonishing uses to which electricity may be put has given the scientific world surprises from time to time, has a new proposal, and one which will arouse widespread interest and comment.
He now proposes to destroy the bacilli of all diseases by applying millions of volts of electricity to persons afflicted. The tremendous force is to be applied in such a manner that the vital organs will be free from harmful effects and so that the bacilli will be drawn from the system.
The tremendous current which Tesla proposes to apply will not be sent through the body, as in the cases of persons executed by electricity, but will run along the surface.
The new plan for destroying disease germs, including even those of consumption, was outlined recently in an exhaustive paper which the electrician read before the Electro-Therapeutic Society, and created deep interest.

In The Electrical Engineer of June 10 , I have noted the description of some experiments of Prof. J. J. Thomson, on the "Electric Discharge in Vacuum Tubes," and in your issue of June 24 Prof. Elihu Thomson describes an experiment of the same kind. The fundamental idea in these experiments is to set up an electromotive force in a vacuum tube — preferably devoid of any electrodes — by means of electro-magnetic induction, and to excite the tube in this manner.

In The Electrical Engineer of August 12 , I find some remarks of Prof. J. J. Thomson, which appeared originally in the London Electrician and which have a bearing upon some experiments described by me in your issue of July 1 .
I did not, as Prof. J. J. Thomson seems to believe, misunderstand his position in regard to the cause of the phenomena considered, but I thought that in his experiments, as well as in my own, electrostatic effects were of great importance. It did not appear, from the meagre description of his experiments, that all possible precautions had been taken to exclude these effects. I did not doubt that luminosity could be excited in a closed tube when electrostatic action is completely excluded. In fact, at the outset, I myself looked for a purely electrodynamic effect and believed that I had obtained it. But many experiments performed at that time proved to me that the electrostatic effects were generally of far greater importance, and admitted of a more satisfactory explanation of most of the phenomena observed.

As was to be expected, the lecture delivered by Mr. Tesla in which he describes the illuminating effects observed in vacuum tubes, has called forth a number of communications from other experimenters who had, it appears, been working in the same direction. Mr. Tesla, it will be remembered, has succeeded in obtaining the effects observed by the employment of very high potential combined with a very high period of alternations, and ascribes the results as due almost, if not entirely, to electro-static action. Prof. J. J. Thomson, in his study of those phenomena, is led to the conclusion that luminosity in tubes without electrodes can be produced by electro-dynamic as well as by electro-static action. In proof of this he cites an experiment in which the electro-static action was ostensibly screened by covering the tube with wet blotting paper. It would seem doubtful, however, whether the precautions taken were sufficiently complete to avoid any electro-static action whatever, and for lack of further proof on this point final judgment may well be suspended. February 25th, 1917
The ideal simplicity of the induction motor, its perfect reversibility and other unique qualities render it eminently suitable for ship propulsion, and ever since I brought my system of power transmission to the attention of the profession through the American Institute of Electrical Engineers I have vigorously insisted on its application for that purpose. During many years the scheme was declared to be impracticable and I was assailed in a manner as vicious as incompetent. In 1900, when an article from me advocating the electric drive appeared in the Century Magazine, Marine Engineering pronounced the plan to be the "climax of asininity," and such was the fury aroused by my proposals that the editor of another technical periodical resigned and severed his connection rather than to allow the publication of some attacks.
A similar reception was accorded to my wireless boat repeatedly described in the Herald of 1898. The patents on these inventions have since expired and they are now common property. Meanwhile insane antagonism and ignorance have been replaced by helpful interest and appreciation of their value. New York, Oct. 5. — Millions of volts of electricity were harnessed the other night in Nikola Tesla’s laboratory and turned into the plaything of men and women. The occasion was a reception given the members of the American Electro-Therapeutic Association by Mr. Tesla.
First was exhibited the machine for generating electricity, invented by Mr. Tesla. This machine looks something like an ordinary turning lathe, and with it a perfect control can be had over the vibration of the electrical current. The velocity of the movement is such that a shadow extending almost two inches from either end of the bar causes an appearance like the bar itself.
After this had been explained everybody was instructed to join a circle around a table which looked like an ordinary dining room article, but was heavily bound with wires. If the beautiful experiments exhibited at the Royal Institution by Mr. Tesla, the able lieutenant of Mr. Edison, are of practical value, and not the mere playthings of the lecture-room, we may be on the eve of some of the greatest discoveries that the world has ever seen. What mankind want during the waking hours of the night is not a glow in the darkness, however intense, but a suffusing, pervading illumination. They want, in fact, sunshine at night. But this, it seems, is what Mr. Tesla is on the eve of offering to us. At his lectures at the Royal Institution, the following striking experiment was shown. It consisted "in joining two sheets of tinfoil, one over the lecturer's head, the other on the table, to the poles of his generator. The space between these two sheets immediately became electrified, and a long vacuum-tube waved about in it, without attachment to any conductor whatever, glowed in the darkness like a flaming sword. This experiment was intended to illustrate the possibility of rendering an entire room so electric, by plates in the ceiling or under the floor, that vacuum-bulbs placed anywhere within it would yield a light." In other words, we shall be able to fill our rooms with the potentiality of light, and then be able, by the simple introduction of vacuum-tubes, to obtain any quantity of light. IS NOW AS CHEAP AS GAS
Wholesale Users Can Get Electricity at Even a Lower Price Than the Older Illuminant.
FURTHER CUTS POSSIBLE.
To meet the reduction in electric light rates made by the Edison Company on October 1, the United Electric Light and Power Company yesterday issued a new schedule, with a rate considerably lower than that of the rival company. This reduction, which will operate on bills for this month, places incandescent lights on the same footing with gas, practically, and large users will get the light even cheaper than gas.
An attempt was made last winter in the Legislature at Albany to make electric light companies lower the price for incandescent lighting from the one cent an hour basis per sixteen candle power lamp to a three-quarters of a cent basis, but the bill did not become a law. Now the companies have made a cut voluntarily.

New York Post
August 16th, 1894

11
America is by far the largest user of electric light, but the methods of production and utilization in use here do not appear to be quite so economical as those practised abroad. The plants throughout Europe are generally on a much more modest scale than here, except in a few such cities as Berlin, Hamburg, and Vienna, yet recent statistics show that some of the smallest are competing successfully, not only with long established gas-works, but with petroleum. Very little of the current, however, is used for power purposes, and conveniences like the fan motors now running daily by the hundred thousand in the United States are well-nigh unknown; so much so that when needed they are shipped from New York. In Berlin 19.9 per cent. of the current is employed in lighting dwellings and hotels, but in Hamburg the same item runs up to 38.7 per cent. Store lighting in the larger German and Austrian cities averages 80 per cent. of the current. Berlin and Vienna use much less than 10 per cent. of the current for driving motors in factories, stores, etc. Exceedingly little use is yet made of the current for heating. A large proportion of the stations have storage-battery equipments; in America this auxiliary is almost unheard of in central-station operation, though nobody appears to know why.

New York, May 27. — Some of the most important devices used for the transmission of electricity for lighting purposes are involved in an application for an injunction to be argued in the United States Circuit Court to-day. The Westinghouse Electric Manufacturing Company is seeking to enjoin The Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company, asserting that patents of Nikola Tesla have been infringed. The counsel who will appear in the argument includes former Speaker Thomas B. Reed, Charles E. Mitchell, formerly United States Commissioner of Patents, and William Houston Kenyon.
The present suit is the seventh one brought to test the validity of these patents, and upon the outcome vast Interests are dependent. The legal papers to be used in the case fill several bulky volumes, going over in great detail the history of the inventions in dispute.

Perhaps We Are on the Verge of Finding a Way to Produce Artificial Sunlight — What Prof. Pupin Can Do with the Current.
Holland in the Philadelphia Press.
Prof. Pupin of Columbia College on Saturday afternoon made some experiments which seemed to experts present quite as interesting and important, although not so brilliant to the eyes, as were those of Nikola Tesla. It was before an assemblage of Columbia College students and experts that Tesla made those experiments a year ago which have given him fame. Prof. Pupin was present and was very greatly impressed by the demonstration which Mr. Tesla made.

Tesla was able to procure an alternating current of vibration sufficient to produce a glow, and, in fact, to create a light in an electric lamp when he held it in his hand and yet without any communication by wire or otherwise with the electric dynamo. Dr. H. R. Humphries, neurologist at the Post Graduate Hospital, does not think very highly of Nikola Tesla's scheme to improve the mental condition of defective children by electric stimulation. As a neurologis for ten years at the Vanderbilt Clinic and for five years at the State Hospital for the Insane, Dr. Humphries has had experience with mental diseases and he feels very strongly on this particular subject.
"As I understand the proposed scheme," he said, "the plan is to charge the walls of the schoolroom where the defective children are with electricity and so to set up in the air a high grade frequency current. It is believed that this current will stimulate the cerebral cells of the defective child and so improve mentality. The proposition is silly.
"In my opinion, based upon years of ob- servations and experiment, there would be no value in such a proceeding. If we thought there was any value in it we could supply every defective child at our hospitals with a skull cap in which could be set up such a high grade frequency current, but we know that there would be no use in trying it. Governor Morton Invited to Attend an Exhibition.
ALBANY, April 9. — Frank W. Hawley was here to-day and extended to Gov. Morton an invitation to be present and officiate at the opening of the National Exposition of Electrical Appliances, to be held at the Grand Central Palace, in the city of New York on May 5th.
The Governor’s part in the great event will be the turning on of a current of electricity generated at the Falls of Niagara and transmitted a distance of 472 miles over one of the commercial wires of the Western Union telegraph, the new “Tesla” system of long distance transmission being employed.
The current will operate a large model of the Niagara power plant and a model of the cable-way system of canal boat propulsion. This is the longest transmission of power ever accomplished. The nearest approach to it was a transmission over a line in Europe 110 miles long.
Another feature of the exposition as explained to the Governor will be the placing of a large receiver at the brink of the Falls and a transmitter in the exposition building, enabling those witnessing the application of this mysterious energy to the movement of machinery to hear the roar of the great cataract that produces it.

An Electrical Convention
New York Times
August 21st, 1889
Page number(s):
2
At the last meeting of the Connell of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers the action of the preceding meeting was reviewed, and instead of a committee of five, the President was directed to appoint a committee of fifteen to form a plan of organization for an international electrical convention to be held in this city coincident with the World's Fair of 1892. Secretary R. W. Pope was instructed to inform President Mascart of the electrical conference at Paris of this action, and to suggest that the unfinished work of the present conference be taken up at the proposed conference of 1892.
The following were elected delegates to represent the institute at the Paris conference now in session: Thomas A. Edison, E. Wilbur Rice, Jr., Carl Hering, Joseph Wetzler, and Nikola Tesla. All of them are now in France or on the way there. President Elihu Thompson will in a few days announce his appointments on the committee of fifteen and the work of organization will then be taken up. An invitation will be extended to all the electrical organizations of the country to participate in the proposed international conference.

Electrical Cure for Skin Disease
New York Herald
October 31st, 1897
Nikola Tesla is now in the midst of intricate electrical experiments which promise most valuable hygienic results, so soon as he declares himself ready to put his recently acquired knowledge into practical operation, for the ridding of the human skin of all extraneous matter, including parasites of every nature, whether they are virulent disease germs or not.
These experiments have been conducted by Mr. Tesla for some time within the secret precincts of his laboratory, and all of the matters involved, from the first inception to the last experiment, have received most careful consideration, and a number of times in his published writings he has hinted at what he believed and what he expected to accomplish, but only incidentally, and in a manner that has made his readers anxious to know just what it is he expects to do and how he intends to accomplish it.
Mr. Tesla was found in his laboratory yesterday, with head and hands full of matters electrical, as usual, and when spoken to of the interest his hints and suggestions of what he was doing had aroused he hesitated for a moment before answering.

Electrical Discovery
Monroe County Mail
August 23rd, 1900
Page number(s):
1
NEW YORK, Aug. 17. — A patent has been granted to Nikola Tesla for an invention which, if his claims are borne out, will prevent the escape of electricity from a wire. Tesla’s invention, it is claimed, solves the insulation problem in a simple manner. He insulates the wire by passing through it or near it air kept at a low temperature, producing a coat of ice on the wire which, the inventor finds by repeated and extensive experiments, cannot be broken through by the strongest currents and at the same time gives an insulation that costs practically nothing.

Brooklyn Eagle

The American Institute of Electrical Engineers will hold its first conversazione in the Engineering Building, Columbia University, Manhattan, this evening. The institute has arranged for the exhibition of many novel inventions, etc., by Clarke, Clift, Croker, Cross, Editor, Hammer, Hewitt, Marconi, Nichols, Perret, Pupin, Ryan, Steinmetz, Tesla, Thomson and Townsend, also by members connected with the General Electric Company, Queen & Co., and the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company.
As most of these exhibits will be shown for the first time, the occasion will be of special interest.

Electrical Exhibition in New York
Cortland Standard
May 15th, 1896
Page number(s):
2
The present electrical exhibition in New York is the most important and interesting of the kind ever held. Among its main features will be exhibited for the first time on a large scale Tesla's invention for telegraphing around the world without a wire or metallic circuit. If it is successful, the world will need no more telegraph poles or ocean cables. Tesla has also succeeded in producing an electrical current of 10,000,000 volts, which he declares is perfectly harmless. The sight of machinery whirling and spinning by means of power brought from Niagara falls, 450 miles away, is enough to make anybody be thankful he lives in this age and generation. Edison's fluoroscope, in which the visitor may see the skeleton frame of his hands and arms, is calculated tο make one feel creepy.

Membership buttons of two of America's oldest radio associations, the Wireless Association of America — the world's first — and the Radio League of America, both organized by Hugo Gernsback.
"Long live the amateur, long live wireless!" shouted the opening article of a new publication, " The Electrical Experimenter ," which had long been pondered but finally was born with the issue of May, 1913. Gernsback had terminated a campaign on the part of the American amateur in Modern Electrics , but he plunged at once into the affairs of hamdom in the Electrical Experimenter by publishing a lengthy but easy-to-read piece on "Building Large Spark Coils." He would not accept or print advertising matter, an announcement said. The periodical — which at 5 cents a copy was said to have been produced at a loss — would be strictly a service to subscribers and customers of the Electro Importing Co.
The assistant editor was Harry Winfield Secor, who had been with Gernsback on Modern Electrics , and who was destined to be a member of the organization — with brief interruptions — to the present day.
Lee de Forest in the June, 1913, Electrical Experimenter told of "Recent Developments at the Federal Telegraph Co." which he said "enjoyed the distinction of having no press agents."

Rochester Democrat and Chronicle
June 19th, 1902
Page number(s):
4
They Expect Edison, Tesla and Pupin at Their Convention
Great Barrington, Mass, June 18. — The first detachment of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, who are to hold their annual convention here the present week, arrived by special train from New York. There were 100 engineers in the party. An additional hundred will arrive when the convention will be called to order in the town hall.
The entire early summer colony turned out to meet the engineers at the railway station. There was an interminable procession of carriages and the local committer, comprising the principal citizens of the town, was kept busy assorting the engineers and sending them away to their respective hotels.
The convention will hold morning sessions daily until Saturday, when the engineers will return to New York, on a special train. It is expected that Thomas A. Edison, Nicola Tesla and Professor Pupin will be present. The Town Hall is beautifully decorated with evergreens and electric bulbs in honor of the occasion.
Many important papers are to be read to the convention and many new theories are to be aired. Among the authors to be heard are several young aspirants to the mantles of Edison, Pupin and Tesla.

New York Post
May 30th, 1896

An Attendance of Quarter of a Million Persons — Some of the Lessons of the Show.
The Electrical Exposition, when it closes to-night, will have been visited by no fewer than a quarter of a million of people, and the managers are simply bewildered at their success. When the exposition was first broached there was great difficulty in arousing interest, and those who were in favor of the scheme were told almost every theatrical manager in the city was on his uppers, and that no show, especially of a technical character, could be run to make money. An Evening Post reporter is informed that when the members of the National Electric Light Association organized their little company to take care of the show, they stipulated that the association should receive $2,000 for the use of its name, and a certain percentage of any profits that might accrue, so that the art as a whole might benefit directly. Even so late, however, as the beginning of the show, when the association held its convention, it was resolved by the officers of the association that in view of the obvious good that would result to the business of electric light and power, and the great likelihood of a failure, the exposition company should not be pressed for the full amount of $2,000. A Electrical Genius
New York Press
April 3rd, 1892
Page number(s):
22
Nikola Tesla was born at Smiljan, a small place on the Austrian border, and is now 35 years of age. His education was received at Carlstadt in Croatia; he showed the experimental beat, and eventually entered the polytechnic school in Gratz, Austria. Here he studied engineering and devoted his spare time to studying electricity. On graduation he entered the engineering department of the telegraph at Budapest. His recent lectures before European authorities and his ingenious electrical inventions have made him famous. His New York laboratory is one of the best equipped in the country.

By Adam Sudetic , Member, Lodge 519
Shown is a collection of some of the late Dr. Nikola Tesla's wireless lamps, such as he once proposed to use in lighting isolated dwellings all over the world from central wireless plants. The two lamps at either corner at the bottom are illuminated, due to the fact that a High Frequency Oscillator was in operation some distance away when this photograph was being taken. These tubes were filled with various gases for experimental research work in determining which was the most efficient. Dr. Tesla died January 7, 1943, in New York.
DETROIT, Mich. — With his Polyphase, Multiphase, etc., system, his Turbines, Generators and Transformers, the late, great Dr. Nikola Tesla revolutionized America's modern industrial might as we know it today.
This alone would place him among the immortals. But he did not stop there. No, he went on to new discoveries and inventions and devoted his life to scientific research with one purpose in mind — to find ways and means to subdue the forces of Mother Nature for the benefit of suffering mankind.

'Electrical Hall of Fame' Urged for Old Adams Plant
Niagara Falls Gazette
July 8th, 1958
Page number(s):
13
A committee of industrial leaders here has started work on a plan to convert the old Edward Dean Adams power plant on the upper river into an "electrical hall of fame."
The committee, organized by James G. Marshall, 88-year old retired Electro Metallurgical Co. works manager, decided at a meeting at Hotel Niagara Monday to make overtures to the federal and state governments, electrical equipment manufacturers and historical societies for help in making the old plant a permanent museum.
The Adams plant is to be taken out of service when the new power plant at Lewiston goes into operation in 1961.
First AC Transmission
It was from the Adams plant in 1895 that alternating current was first transmitted over a long distance. Power from the Adams plant was used to illuminate the new street lights in Buffalo — 25 miles away.

Half-tone Picture Transmitted by Wire from Chicago to New York.
NEW YORK, April 13. — Two bodies of scientific men gathered last night — one in Columbia College, this city, and the other in the rooms of the Quadrangle in Chicago, to witness the test of an electrical Instrument which was to transmit the half-tone picture by wire of President Seth Low to the Chicagoans and that of President Harris to the New Yorkers. The experiment was a success at the New York end, and 8,000 people gathered in the hall and watched the features of the President of the Chicago University evolve out of a maze of pin points in tin foil till it became a facsimile of the one on the transmitter, 1,000 miles away.
Chicagoans Disappointed
The Chicago audience however, according to word received by telegraph, was disappointed. The instrument at that end did not work because of heavy Induction in the wires.
R. H. Palmer operated the electrical machine transmitting the picture. The instrument contains tin foil perforated with countless pin holes each containing a separate wire. The paper upon which the picture is produced is wrapped around a cylinder upon which the sensitive tin foil stylus makes the ink dots corresponding in light and shade to the half-tone picture being transmitted.

The wonders of electricity have often been discussed with lively interest. This has been called the electrical age, because of the extraordinary developments in applying the subtle current to practical and beneficent purposes. Electrical Phenomena
Progressive Batavian
1893
In one of his remarkable lectures, Tesla states that most scientific men now look upon the various forms of manifestations of energy, which are generally designated "electric," as energy manifestations of the same nature as those of radiant heat and light. The phenomena of light and heat, and others besides, may therefore be called electrical phenomena, and thus it is that electrical science has become the mother science of all, and its study all-important. The day when we shall know exactly what electricity is will chronicle an event probably greater and of more moment than any other recorded in the history of the human race.

Electrical Possibilities. It is not an extravagant statement to say that never before in the history of the world has there been a scientific discovery about which centered such magnificent dreams as are being built up on certain recently discovered electrical principles. "Among these the foremost place," says the Springfield Republican , must be given to the astounding discoveries of the young Serbian genius, Nikola Tesla, which are so novel and so extraordinary that the most imaginative of inventors are unable to foresee what form their development will take. Just as experimenters were beginning to think that they knew all that could be learned about electricity, and that further improvement must be in the line of more perfect mechanical application, Mr. Tesla shows us the electric fluid under conditions in which it differs from ordinary electricity as much as light differs from heat. A current of 2,000 volts will kill a man in the twinkling of an eye, but this modern wizard lets currents pour through his hands with a potential of 200,000 volts, vibrating 1,000,000 times a second and showering from him in dazzling streams of light. For some time after the experiment ceases his body and clothing emit streams and halos of splintered light.

Tesla's latest invention, the "Oscillator," is described as one of the most remarkable appliances of the age, consisting of "the core of a steam engine and the core of a dynamo combined, making a harmonious mechanical adjustment." This combination, says an enthusiastic admirer, constitutes a machine which has in it the potentiality of reducing to the rank of old bell metal half the machinery at present moving on the face of the globe. It may come to do the entire work of the engines of an ocean steamship within the small space they occupy and at a fraction of their cost, both of construction and operation. It will do this work without jar or pounding, and will reduce to a minimum the risk of derangement or breakage. There is nothing in the whole range of mechanical construction, from railway locomotives to stamp mills, which such an invention may not revolutionize. The essential characteristic of the machine is the application of the pressure of steam to produce the extremely rapid vibration of a bar of steel, or piston, which, in turn, is so adapted to a set of magnets that the mechanical energy of the vibration is converted into electricity. Mr. Edison sat at the principal place at the speakers’ table to-day, while an American flag was removed from a pedestal before him, exposing the perfect cube of copper, weighing 486 pounds. It is the first block of that size ever cast and required six castings to produce the perfect specimen, beautifully finished and engraved, and mounted on an ebony pedestal.
Some time ago, when conversing with some representatives of the copper industry, Mr. Edison jokingly remarked that they ought to present him with some token to show their appreciation of his inventions having boomed the sale of copper. An Electrical Wizard
Utica Sunday Tribune
March 19th, 1893
Nikola Tesla Allows a Charge of 200,000 Volts to Pass Through His Body.
"I am convinced that I can today send a message to a ship at sea, and that those on board can understand it. If I cannot, I am willing to lay my head on the guillotine."
Nikola Tesla.
It was Nikola Tesla who made the above strange remark, and his wonderful achievements in the development of electrical science make his words worthy of respectful consideration. He has already established the fact that but one wire is necessary to create an electrical current and is now engaged on the problem of transmitting a current without the use of a wire at all. That he has grasped the secret of how this may ultimately be accomplished some of the experiments exhibited at his public lectures would seem to demonstrate.
Tesla produces a distinct and powerful glow without the aid of wires or globes and with apparatus remarkable chiefly for its simplicity. This consists of two highly charged disks; between which the light appears without a connecting fila ment of any kind. In an incandescent lamp hung on a single wire, but not connected with it, he produces a red light almost blinding in its brilliancy, which becomes a powerful white on increasing the frequency of alternations in the current. Electrical World
February 15th, 1890
Page number(s):
106
While a large portion of the European family has been surging westward during the last three or four hundred years, settling the vast continents of America, another, but smaller, portion has been doing frontier work in the Old World, protecting the rear by beating back the "unspeakable Turk" and reclaiming gradually the fair lands that endure the curse of Mohammedan rule. For a long-time the Slav people - who, after the battle of Kosovopolje, in which the Turks defeated the Servians, retired to the confines of the present Montenegro, Dalmatia, Herzegovina and Bosnia and "Borderland" of Austria - knew what it was to deal, as our Western pioneers did, with foes ceaselessly fretting against their frontier; and the races of these countries through their strenuous struggle against the armies of the Crescent, have developed notable qualities of bravery and sagacity, while maintaining a patriotism and independence unsurpassed in any other nation.
It was in this interesting border region and from among these valiant Eastern folk that Nikola Tesla was born; and the fact that he, to-day, finds himself in America and is one of our foremost electricians is striking evidence of the extraordinary attractiveness alike of electrical pursuits and of the country where electricity enjoys its widest application.

In the Electrical World - Tesla's Remarkable Lecture
Progressive Batavian
1893
In one of his remarkable lectures, Tesla states that most scientific men now look upon the various forms of manifestations of energy, which are generally designated “electric,” as energy manifestations of the same nature as those of radiant heat and light. The phenomena of light and heat, and others besides, may therefore be called electrical phenomena, and then it is that electrical science has become the mother science of all, and its study all-important. The day when we shall know exactly what electricity is will chronicle an event probably greater and of more moment than any other recorded in the history of the human race.

Electricians in This City Regard the Hunter Patents as Amusing
New York Herald
December 22nd, 1897
Page number(s):
3
Electricians in this city do not take Rudolph M. Hunter seriously. They say he will patent anything regardless of its practicability, and probably ranks seventh among men and corporations in the number of his patented electrical devices. He is credited with having taken out more than four hundred patents.
I explained to Nikola Tesla, in his laboratory at No. 46 East Houston street, yesterday. Mr. Hunter's latest patents. He was greatly amused.
"I could tell a whole lot about Mr. Hunter and his numerous patents," he said, "but it might appear that I am antagonistic to him, which is not so.
"His contention that his patents cover the alternating principle of transmitting electrical energy is silly. This method dates too far back to be patented as a system. I do not think his claims will prove an important factor in the electrical world or a disturbing element in the methods now in use."
At the offices of the Westinghouse Company, No. 120 Broadway. Mr. Hunter's patents were treated as amusing.
"We know Mr. Hunter very well," said Mr. Terry, the patent attorney of the company. "These transformer patents amount to little. We own six thousand of the ten thousand patents covering electrical devices. We are working under them and shall continue to work under them."

Tesla Gives Demonstrations of His Latest Invention.
TRANSMITTING PICTURES BY WIRE
Test Fails Because of Induction, but Success Hoped for Today — Edison and John D. Rockefeller Present.
Of more than usual interest to the general public is the conversazione held yesterday in Columbia University by the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. Many new and important inventions were shown and original and interesting experiments were made. The exhibits fill twelve rooms and represent the work of fifty eminent scientists. Among them is Nikola Tesla.
Interest last night centred in an effort to transmit pictures to distant cities by wire. The receiving point was the University of Chicago. The test failed, so it was reported from Chicago.
The instrument, or electrograph, had worked successfully across distances of several hundred miles, but last night, owing to induction of the wires in New York, would not record the thousand of fine dots of which the pictures are composed. It was proposed to transmit between the two cities pictures of President William R. Harper of the University of Chicago, President Seth Low of Columbia and John D. Rockefeller.
PROMINENT FOLK PRESENT.

In place of the tape of narrow paper a continuous roll a little wider than two columns of the Sun is automatically fed in front of this wheel and prints in a broad line of clear type whatever the matter is that is to be published. This roll of news can be 2 inches, 2 feet or two yards long, or any other length desired. An expert telegrapher is now needed to send out the messages, which are printed simultaneously on all the instruments on the circuit. Electricity and Disease
Oswego Daily Palladium
January 28th, 1896
Page number(s):
4
There may be something in the report that Nikola Tesla has discovered a way in which diseases may be shaken out of the human system by electricity. Last week a New York electrician accidentally made himself a conductor for a current of electricity with an estimated strength of 2,000 volts, or 300 more volts than is developed by the machines at Sing Sing which electrocute condemned murderers. As will be seen by the account printed of the accident printed on our seventh page to-day, the electrician was thrown into convulsions by the shock, and for an entire day his life hung in the balance. But when he recovered he pronounced himself as feeling better than he did before the accident. He is experiencing a feeling of rejuvenation, like that which follows a long rest, and has lost a stubborn case of rheumatism which was the cause of much pain and suffering.
While the victim of the electrical accident was slowly recovering his equilibrium, the section on general medicine of the New York Academy of Medicine was discussing “The Theory and Treatment of Rheumatism,” and expressing opinions as to the cause of the disease. This discussion revealed the fact that the medical profession is inclining to the belief that rheumatism is caused by bacteria in the blood. Electricity and Wires
Yonkers Statesman
August 31st, 1900
Page number(s):
1
A patent has been granted to Nikola Tesla for an invention which, if his claims are borne out, will prevent the escape of electricity from a wire. Tesla's invention, it is claimed, solves the insulation problem in a simple manner. He insulates the wire by passing through it, or near it, air kept at a low temperature, producing a coat of ice on the wire, which, the inventor finds, cannot be broken through by the strongest current, and at the same time gives an insulation that costs practically nothing. By means of this latest discovery the loss of electricity or electrical energy in transmission, it is claimed, can be rendered so small as to be insignificant, and power can be transmitted to great distances by means of underground wires.

Electricity on the Canal
Clyde Democratic Herald
November 8th, 1893
The test of electricity as a motor power on the canals of the State will probably be made at Pittsford on the Erie Canal near Rochester, Saturday, November 11th. The pole line is already completed and the generators and electrical appliances have been shipped from Pittsburg to Pittsford. The experiment will be witnessed by State officials, officers of the Niagara Power Company and officers of the Westinghouse Electrical Company, who will arrive at Pittsford at 9 a. m. on the day of the experiment, on a West Shore special train leaving New York at 10 o’clock the night before.
Mr. F. W. Hawley, who is actively interested in the experiment and whose residence is at Pittsford, received a dispatch this morning to the effect that the experimental boat, the first electrical canal boat ever built, is at Buffalo. It will probably reach Pittsford Monday. Nikola Tesla, the great Hungarian electrician from Budapest, and George Forbes, the celebrated English electrician, will be present to study this new application of electricity.

Electricity from Coal
New York Globe
November 26th, 1904
Page number(s):
3
The Dynelectron and Other Carbon Batteries — A Long Series of Failures — Attempts by Tesla and Edison — The Probability of Eventual Success.
The revolutionary character and vast financial possibilities of a practical commercial battery producing electricity directly from coal, without the intervention of boiler and steam engine, is obvious enough to the merest tyro in mechanics. Theoretically, such a coal battery might have an efficiency of something like 70 per cent., whereas existing methods of producing electrical energy, according to W. R. Cooper, only render available 6 per cent. of the energy of the coal. This fact, combined with the possibility of greatly reducing the cost of an electric plant, through the elimination of engines, boilers, and a number of the skilled workmen necessary to keep them in running order, makes the coal battery an intensely fascinating problem for the inventor.
However, despite the numerous attempts made to solve it, only dismal failure has hitherto been the result. The latest of these is called by its inventor, J. H. Reid of Newark, N. J., the dynelectron. This machine and Mr. Reid himself are described at considerable length in the October number of the Marconigram. From the facts stated there the dynelectron seems to be, in its essentials, an iron box divided into three compartments. In two of these caustic soda is placed.

Chautauquan
September, 1897
BY FRANZ BENDT.
TRANSLATED FOR "THE CHAUTAUQUAN" FROM THE GERMAN "UEBER LAND UND MEER."
It is mostly through its practical results that a science appeals to the general public for anything more than a casual attention. This fact is nowhere more noticeable than in electricity, which has loaded humanity with gifts and in a comparatively short time has revolutionized customs and business so that the present era not unjustly has been called "the age of electricity." The term is doubly appropriate because, as all signs indicate, we are not at the end but only just at the beginning of the electrical epoch. Moreover, it should be noted, the wonderful and mysterious manner in which the electrical forces are manifested have thoroughly aroused astonishment, even in adepts, and a thirst for knowledge in the laity.
In glancing over the many practical acquisitions of the young science one gets the impression that for its years it has developed strongly and powerfully, if also disproportionately. Yet many branches of the electrical science have broadened out into mighty industries. Electricity Lectures at the World's Fair School
Chicago Columbian
July 15th, 1893
Page number(s):
1
The following will be the weekly schedule of lectures upon the Electricity Department of the World’s Fair. They will be delivered at 10 o’clock each day in the Agricultural Assembly Hall by Prof. Gooch.
On Mondays there will be discussed the principles of primary batteries, storage batteries, electric furnace, electro-plating, electric engraving, and Edison’s last invention, the Kinetograph.
Tuesdays — The telegraph, telephone, phonograph, telautograph, Atlantic cable system, and cooking and heating.
Wednesdays — Edison system of lighting.
Thursdays — The alternating system and Nikola Tesla’s theory of utilizing the power of Niagara Falls.
Fridays — Arc lighting, welding and drilling.
Saturdays — Electric street car system.
The purpose of the lectures is to give an intelligent understanding of the principles of the various apparatus on exhibition, the manner of their construction and practical operation. The class is open to all persons who desire an explanation of the wonderful developments of electricity and the various applications to which it may be adapted.

Electricity - The Power Transmission System of Gold King Mill in Telluride
by Franklin L. Pope
Engineering Magazine
August, 1892
Page number(s):
710-711
An interesting example of electric-power transmission is that of the Gold King stamp-mill near Telluride, Col. A Pelton wheel, receiving water through a two-foot steel pipe under 320 feet head, drives the generator at a speed of 833 revolutions, giving 10,000 alternations per minute. The generator, by an automatic compensation, is made to maintain a constant pressure of 3000 volts at the motor, three miles distant. The line runs 2500 feet directly up the mountain from the power station, and thence passes over a rough, and in winter almost inaccessible, country, to the mill. The working motor, being of the synchronous type, requires a special device for starting it, and this is furnished by a small auxiliary motor of the Tesla type. The operation of starting is accomplished by one man in about two minutes. The economical efficiency of the synchronous motor system, exclusive of loss in conductors, is found to be 83.5 per cent. at full load and 74 per cent. at half load. The capacity of the motor is 50 horse-power. How the "Electric Subjugator" Shocks a Lion into Submission When He Attacks the Trainer in His Cage.
To the Editor of the Journal:
It seems to me that there are interesting possibilities in the training of animals by electricity. Of course, it's rather out of my province, but the idea of the electrical subjugator appears feasible when one knows the power of electricity and the instinctive fear that brutes have of the unknown. And the electrical method seems more humane than those I believe are in use — the whip, red hot irons, and drugs, which are likely to do permanent injury, while the physical effects of an electric shock are soon gone, only the moral ones remaining.
The subjugator referred to will do the work, but I think an apparatus could be designed that would be less dangerous to the man. I do not desire to be understood as giving the matter deep thought, but believe that if instead of the armored backpad, the trainer used a wand, with two prongs at one end, better results would follow. Nikola Tesla Says the Carbon Demonstrations of Mr. Case Are Not New.
Willard E. Case's announcement before the New York Electrical Society at Columbia College that he can produce electricity from carbon without heat has caused some stir among the men who are devoting their time to the development of electricity.
He cited the fact that the generation of energy through heat involves a waste of more than 75 per cent, and that all electricity except that produced by water power or galvanic battery is obtained ultimately from carbon.
Nikola Tesla was seen to-day and asked what his views were concerning Mr. Case's new road to electricity.
"The process of converting the energy of combining carbon and oxygen with electricity without any loss in the battery is not new," he said, "It has been observed that In the process there is no weakening of temperature shown, consequently there seems to be no loss in heat.
"In my opinion this does not show at all there is no loss in reaching a combination. On the contrary, I am convinced that the second law of thermo-dynamics is far more general than it is believed to be. As long, however, as we contine ourselves to developing energy by consuming material we are adhering to barbarous processes which imply destruction and waste.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD: —
In reply to your question as to what discovery would do most to better our condition, in my opinion the demonstration that the earth's electrical charge can be distributed, and thereby electrical waves efficiently transmitted to any distance without the use of cables or wires, would be the most beneficial.
The conveying of motive power from sources such as Niagara in this manner to any place, however remote, would increase many times the productive capacity of mankind. It would bring millions of miserable creatures from the darkness of the coal pits to the light of day. It would cause a kinder feeling to spring up between the weak and the strong, which would lead to a generous adjustment of the evermore difficult questions of labor and capital.
Even if power could not be distributed, the mere transmission of intelligible signals would be of incalculable benefit. It would greatly facilitate the evolution of novel ideas, as well as the prevention of evils. It would increase the safety of travel and give a new impetus to the press and spread of knowledge. Awards formed the principal topic of discussion among the electrical exhibitors at the World's Fair last week. The exclusive publication of the list in the Western Electrician excited much interest, and the paper was in great demand. The comments were many and varied. Some exhibitors were jubilant; others were angry and disgusted, while not a few professed indifference, with the remark, "What do the awards amount to, anyway?" It was noticeable, however, that all seemed eager to secure the diplomas and medals before the list was posted. Many, also, were puzzled by the fact that several awards, in a number of cases, were given on one class of apparatus. This is explained by the fact that the judges did not consider the comparative merits of. exhibits in making awards. They examined each exhibit entered for an award separately, and if, in, their judgment, the article or group was found to be worthy of commendation an award was given it, the specific points of excellence being detailed in the diploma. It thus happened that on the commoner sorts of apparatus, such as arc lamps, for instance, a number of awards were given on the same class of exhibits, although the exact language of the awards, specifying the points of excellence, will not be alike on any two diplomas. Aside from several distinguished members of the congress who remained to see the exposition, two notable figures attracted attention in the electricity building last week — Thomas A. Edison and Nikola Tesla. Mr. Edison paid several visits to the building, strictly in the capacity of a spectator, and greatly enjoyed his inspection of the exhibits. Mr. Tesla gave a number of experiments before invited guests and the general public. On Tuesday afternoon he repeated, at the agricultural assembly hall, the substance of his lecture on "Mechanical and Electrical Oscillators," which was delivered before the members of the congress on the preceding Friday. On this occasion he had for an audience von Helmholtz and a number of other scientists who had been unable to attend the first lecture. On Tuesday evening Mr. Tesla repeated his beautiful and interesting high tension and high frequency experiments in the dark pavilion of the Westinghouse company in electricity building before a number of foreign engineers, including W. H. Preece, H. D. Wilkinson, MM. Mascart and de la Touanne, Dr. Lobach, F. W. Tischendoerfer and others. Electricity's New Marvels
New York Press
April 18th, 1896
Many Will Be Seen at the National Exhibition Next Month.
Many interesting features have been arranged for the opening of the National Electric Exhibition on May 4 at the Grand Central Palace. Governor Morton has been asked to officiate. Electric power will be sent by the Tesla system over a Western Unton wire from Niagara Falls, a distance of 462 miles. The power will be used for the operation of a model of the Niagara power system, as well as for sending a message of congratulation from the President to Queen Victoria on her birthday.
The lines of the Portal Telegraph and Cabie Company will be offered for the transmission of the Niagara power across the continent.

Portville Review
October 17th, 1912
The secret of the universe is the secret of electricity.
"The New Knowledge" is the term used for designating the revelations which came with the study of radium and radio-activity. "The New Knowledge" has taught us that matter — lead, stone, wood, hydrogen, oxygen, everything and anything which we call matter — is nothing but electricity.
An atom of hydrogen consists of a thousand "electrons" — mere charges of electricity. An atom of lead consists of some hundreds of thousands of such "electrons'. That is why hydrogen is so light and lead so heavy. Each is drawn to that great mass of matter, the earth, in proportion to the number of electric charges which make up the earth. That is the law of gravitation. It is all a question of electricity.
We ourselves are nothing but collections of "electron" of many sorts. The rose in the bosom of beauty, and the bone in the jaws of the Beast, are like the Beauty and the Beast, nothing but greater or lesser, simpler or more complex collection of "electrons" or electric charges. Matter studied closely vanishes in matterless electricity.

To Electrify Children
New York Sun
July 31st, 1912
Page number(s):
14
Tesla Will Try to Get Permission for Stockholm Experiments Here.
William H. Maxwell, City Superintendent of Schools, will ask the Board of Education when it meets in the fall to sanction an experiment in electrifying a school room for the purpose of stimulating mentally defective children. Nikola Tesla, the inventor, who is the originator of the idea, has been conferring with Mr. Maxwell and Dr. L. B. Blan and has succeeded in winning them over to the project. Mr. Tesla says that the plan has been tried in Stockholm and that it was found practicable there.
First of all Mr. Maxwell had to be assured that the experiment could not possibly harm the children, and Tesla convinced him that there was no such chance. The apparatus is installed in the walls of the room which is selected for the experiment and is hidden so that neither the children nor the teacher know that it is there. Mr. Maxwell wants to put a class of about fifty deficient children in such a room and to place another similar class at the end of the corridor in an ordinary room as a check on the experiment. At the end of a certain time the records of the two classes will be compared, and in that way the efficiency of the apparatus will be determined.
If the Board of Education approves of the plan Mr. Tesla will personally superintend the installation of the apparatus.

Electro-Motors
by Nikola Tesla
Electrical Review
April 3rd, 1891
Page number(s):
446
Fifteen or sixteen years ago, when I was pursuing my course at the college, I was told by an eminent physicist that a motor could not be operated without the use of brushes and commutators, or mechanical means of some kind for commutating the current. It was then I determined to solve the problem.
After years of persistent thought I finally arrived at a solution. I worked out the theory to the last detail, and confirmed all of my theoretical conclusions by experiments. Recognizing the value of the invention, I applied myself to the work of perfecting it, and after long continued labor I produced several types of practical motors.
Now all this I did long before anything whatever transpired in the whole scientific literature — as far as it could be ascertained — which would have even pointed at the possibility of obtaining such a result, but quite contrary at a time when scientific and practical men alike considered this result unattainable. In all civilized countries patents have been obtained almost without a single reference to anything which would have in the least degree rendered questionable the novelty of the invention. The first published essay — an account of some laboratory experiments by Prof. Ferraris — was published in Italy six or seven months after the date of filing of my applications for the foundation patents. If a delicately and pivoted and well-balanced metal disc or cylinder be placed in a proper plating solution midway between the anode and cathode, one half of the disc becomes electro positive and the other half electro negative. Owing to this fact metal is deposited on one, and taken off from the other half, and the disc is caused to rotate under the action of gravity. As the amount of metal deposited and taken off is proportionate to the current strength, the speed of rotation, if it be small, is proportionate to the current.

by Elsa Maxwell
New York Post
December 30th, 1942

One of the great new developments of modern years is electronics—the science of the movement of the electron through gaseous tubes.
I know this sounds like a mouthful. It also sounds unimportant. But in this strange and relativistic world, it is really the fantastic, the microscopic and the unbelievable which is important. I happen to be very much interested in the electron; and I’m interested for the same reason that I’m interested in Bach, Cézanne, steak Chateaubriand and pandas. The electron is part of the slipstream of living.
Look at what we , with our uniquely American mechanical genius, are doing: We are taking the almost-imperceptible electron, slipping it into harness, sending it up to detect airplanes, sending it down from airplanes to detect submarines, shooting it through smokestacks to detect and measure tell-tale smoke.

Lord Kelvin.
Lord Kelvin, better known as Sir William Thomson, for he was sixty-eight years old and had many years of scientific eminence behind him when he was raised to the English peerage in 1892, arrived in New York recently, on his way to the meeting of the British Association in Toronto. He was met, of course, by a number of reporters, and said the usual polite things in the resulting interviews. More interesting than these is the opinion of the great English scientist expressed by Nikola Tesla, as reported by James Creelman for the New York Journal . Said Mr. Tesla:

He occupies a unique position in the scientific world, not only by reason of his achievements, but also by the fact that he has been active and productive during a period seldom allotted to workers in scientific fields. Usually the efforts of the mind prematurely consume the man. On the possibilities of a global system for the production and transmission of electrical energy
Today, a range of possibilities are being considered for ensuring the necessary quantities of electrical energy in the long term, and a global system for its production and transmission. By positioning three large artificial satellites at 38,000 km from Earth, which would be relatively stationary in relation to the Earth, platforms in space would be obtained. On these, in two phases for the near and distant future, stations of enormous power would be built for supplying the entire world with electrical energy. Engineers are Interested in Tesla's New Turbine
Syracuse Post-Standard
December 6th, 1911
E. F. Stearns in The Popular Mechanics Magazine.
Engineers and men of science throughout the world are awaiting with unusual interest the completion of tests of a new steam turbine designed by Nikola Tesla, which preliminary experiments indicate will give enormous power from a comparatively small and extremely lightweight engine.
Ten horsepower to a pound of weight has already been developed with the engines that have been tested. And enthusiasts who have witnessed the work of the turbine declare the perfect rotor has at last been found. To what extent this is true, time and the construction of larger units than have yet been used must prove.
At present, while the practical experimental stage has not yet been passed, the entire engineering world is profoundly interested in the work that has been done and awaits future development with much concern.

June 30th, 1888

In our issue of the 18th May, we gave an account of a very interesting investigation made by Professor Galiles Ferraris, of Turin, which had for its object the production of mechanical rotation by the electro-dynamic action of alternating currents. The fundamental principle of the apparatus devised by Ferraris, is a revolving resultant magnetic field produced by two coils, which carry alternating currents, and the axes of which are at right angles to each other. We said in our account of this investigation, that this principle may be applied in the construction of electricity meters to be used on an alternate current supply system, and possibly also in that of motors; though on this point we would not prophesy. It is significant of the enterprise and inventive skill of American electricians, that at the time these lines were being printed, Mr. Nicola [ sic ] Tesla brought before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers an actual solution of the problem which we on this side of the Atlantic merely foreshadowed as possible at some future time. Chemistry — Dr. Richard Willstaetter, of the University of Berlin. Physics Divided between Prof. William Henry Bragg of the University of Leeds, and his son, W. L Bragg of Cambridge University, for research in the structure of crystals by use of the Roentgen Rays.
A Copenhagen dispatch to the London Daily Telegraph, Nov. 6, stated that the Swedish Government had decided on the recipients of some of the Nobel prizes, naming Thomas A. Edison and Nikola Tesla to divide the prize in physics, while Prof. Theodore Svedberg was to receive the prize in chemistry.

New York Herald
January 6th, 1898
Tesla with His Perfected Vacuum Takes Photographs as Well by Night as by Day
No More "Flash" Pictures
Powerful Rays Reveal Every Line in the Subject Photographed with Startling Distinctness.
TO ILLUMINE LIGHTHOUSES.
This Picture Was Reproduced from a Photograph Made by the Light of a Single Vacuum Tube, at a Distance of Five Feet, Exposure Five Seconds.
Nikola Tesla, the well known electrician, announces an important discovery to-day in the Electrical Review. He says that he has perfected vacuum tubes of such high illuminating power that they may be used in lighthouses, and that they will enable the photographer to work by night as well as by day. He even suggests that by means of this light the painter may be able to distinguish colors as well at night as he can by the clear, soft light of day.
The result which Mr. Tesla has attained represents several years of patient experimenting. His work was somewhat retarded by the burning of his laboratory in 1895. He is not ready yet to describe his invention in detail. He promises to do soon. He always speaks in a conservative way of his discoveries. I called yesterday at his laboratory. His bearing was one of great elation.
"It is of more importance," he said, "to discover new principles, to find out scientific facts, than to invent mere appliances."

Escapes Jury Duty
Rochester Democrat and Chronicle
October 16th, 1902
Page number(s):
1
Nikola Tesla Does Not Believe in Electrocution as Death Penalty.
Special Dispatch to Democrat and Chronicle
New York, Oct. 15. — The “wizard of electricity,” Nikola Tesla, was in court today as a prospective juror in a murder trial before Judge Warren W. Foster, in General Sessions.
When asked by Assistant District Attorney Ely if he believed in “capital punishment, electrocution,” he replied:
“I indeed do not. It is a barbarous measure. I would never condemn a fellow-being to death.”
Mr. Tesla was excused from jury duty. “I believe in upholding the laws of the country,” he said, while leaving the court room, “but I never could condemn a fellow-being to death.”

William Terbo (Trbojević), Nikola Tesla’s closest living relative
"He was indeed an eccentric, especially in later life, but it seems to me that he himself did a lot to encourage certain beliefs about his eccentricity . . . In essence, he was a philosopher. Not in a theoretical sense, so much as in essence."
Nikola Tesla’s closest relative, a descendant of his sister Jelena, married Trbojević, bears the name William Terbo and strives with all his strength, as the honorary chairman of the "Tesla Memorial Society," to preserve the memory of his great ancestor, of whom not only his kin and the countries where he lived are proud, but the entire world. This non-political and non-profit society aims to preserve and continue the memory and ideals of the great scientist and inventor Nikola Tesla through appropriate academic conferences, school scholarships, and other cultural activities.

The great scholar of ours who has glorified our name, of Serbs and Croats throughout the world, Nikola Tesla, is by birth from the rugged Lika. He was born of Serbian parents in 1856 in the Lika village of Smiljan, in Smiljan. He attended the first grades of higher school gymnasium in Gospić, and he finished the real school in Karlovac, already showing at that time a great will for technology and various useful inventions.
In the first years he went through all the gorges of lamentation until finally he rose by himself with his genius and after many studies and difficult years of trials he decided to go to the New World, to attempt to realize his great ideas in the United States. In the end he succeeded in founding a laboratory in New York in 1887 under his own name "Electric Company Tesla".
Tesla began his schooling in the study of technology in Styrian Graz, which he finished in Prague, Czechia 1881. As a graduated engineer he served at the Telephone Company in Budapest, and later at Edison's Continental Company in Paris.

Evolves New Theories
New York Times
January 18th, 1919
Page number(s):
11
Tesla Says Wireless Waves Pass Through the Earth, Not the Air.
The forthcoming issue of The Electrical Experimenter will contain an article by Nikola Tesla, Inventor, in which he takes issue with the generally accepted theories of the moon's axial rotation, the pointed lightning rod, and the passage of wireless messages through the air.
Dr. Tesla says that "the moon does rotate, not on its own, but about an axis passing through the centre of the earth, the true and only one." He says that wireless messages pass directly through the earth itself, instead of following the earth's curvature through the air, between stations of any great distance apart. He believes that some day there will be a great station that will keep the earth charged with just enough electricity to make wireless sending very simple. Disagreeing with Franklin that the pointed lightning rod makes surrounding air attractive to heavenly bolts, Dr. Tesla says that he has invented a rod with rounded surface which repels lightning.

Ewing's High Frequency Alternator
Electrical World
December 17th, 1892
Page number(s):
391
Prof. Ewing, whose tests of the Parsons steam turbine were published in our last issue , recently designed a high frequency alternator adapted to be driven by this high speed turbine. The complete apparatus, consisting of a steam turbine, alternator and a continuous current dynamo, all direct coupled and on the same base plate, was recently presented by Mr. Parsons to the Cambridge Laboratory.
Figs. 1 & 2 — Field magnet and armature poles.
The alternator has a speed of 1,200 revolutions per minute, and generates currents of 70 complete cycles per revolution, making 14,000 complete cycles per second; the output is about five amperes at 100 volts. The machine is intended for experimental purposes and investigation, among others those of the physiological effects of high frequency alternating currents. Exhibition of Electric Wonders
Yonkers Statesman
April 23rd, 1896
The Electric Exposition, to be held at the Grand Central Palace, next month, will have several features of almost sensational interest, and all the latest electrical marvels will be shown. The exposition, as a whole, will be modeled after that held in Philadelphia in 1884, and the general manager will be C. E. Stump, who was connected with the direction of the Philadelphia display. Although 12 years have elapsed, during which two world's fairs have been held, one at Paris and the other at Chicago, and although electricity has made immense strides since then, yet the Philadelphia exhibition still remains as the most satisfactory display in that department of science that has ever been made.
The coming exhibition will be what its Philadelphia predecessor was a complete exhibition, historically, scientifically, mechanically and commercially, of the development of electricity in all its applications down to the present hour. It will be opened by Governor Morton striking a golden key at Albany, and the electric current will be transmitted over Postal wires to San Francisco and back again to the hall of the exposition. The golden key used will be the same touched by President Cleveland in opening the Chicago Fair.

Exhibition a Monument to the Inventive Genius of Nikola Tesla
Putnam County Republican
June 6th, 1896
The exhibition inaugurated in New York by the National Electric Light Association places another milestone in the wonderful progress of electricity and is a monument also to the inventive genius of Nikola Tesla. His faith in the accuracy of his scientific deductions and the confidence he inspired in a few capitalists are responsible for the transformation of the Falls of Niagara into a gigantic engine for the use of mankind. When Gov. Morton pressed the golden key in the exposition building and released the current generated 462 miles away it typified to the world that the mind of man had brought into absolute subjection this phenomenal concentration of nature’s forces. All the other evidences of electrical progress that appear in the exhibition are insignificant compared to this overwhelming manifestation of the harnessed waterfall and the possibilities of transmitting its power to individual consumers at will. Experiments with Alternating Currents of High Frequency
by Nikola Tesla
Electrical Engineer
March 18th, 1891
Page number(s):
336-337
In The Electrical Engineer issue of 11th inst., I find a note of Prof. Elihu Thomson relating to some of my experiments with alternating currents of very high frequency.
Prof. Thomson calls the attention of your readers to the interesting fact that he has performed some experiments in the same line. I was not quite unprepared to hear this, as a letter from him has appeared in the Electrician a few months ago, in which he mentions a small alternate current machine which was capable of giving, I believe, 5,000 alternations per second, from which letter it likewise appears that his investigations on that subject are of a more recent date.
Prof. Thomson describes an experiment with a bulb enclosing a carbon filament which was brought to incandescence by the bombardment of the molecules of the residual gas when the bulb was immersed in water "rendered slightly conducting by salt dissolved therein," (?) and a potential of 1,000 volts alternating 5,000 time a second applied to the carbon strip. Similar experiments have, of course, been performed by many experimenters, the only distinctive feature in Prof. Thomson's experiment being the comparatively high rate of alternation. Experiments with Alternating Currents of High Frequency - Lecture Abstract - Part 1
Industries
June 5th, 1891
Page number(s):
546
The recent meeting of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers will long be remembered by those present, not only on account of the brilliant experiments shown in connection with a lecture given by Mr. Nikola Tesla, but also for the many possibilities which it suggested in the development of the artificial illumination of the future. For the purpose of his experiments, Mr. Tesla employed an alternating machine with 400 poles, which, when run at full speed, permitted him to obtain 20,000 alternations per second. The currents of this machine in all of Mr. Tesla's experiments were first run through a condenser in order to avoid the possibility of injury to the machine. The machine itself was set up in the electrical workshop of the college, and was driven by an electric motor, the speed of which could be varied by a switch on the lecture platform.
Mr. Tesla introduced his subject by the remark that modern science has been able to make rapid strides by the recognition of ether as the medium of transmission of vibrations of various forms which manifest themselves to our senses. Professor Pupin Obtains Gratifying Results in the Laboratory of Columbia College.
SEVERAL GOOD PICTURES.
The Bones of a Hand, Nails in a Box and the Cogwheels of a Watch Faithfully Reproduced.
HINTS FOR EXPERIMENTERS.
In the laboratory at Columbia College yesterday afternoon Professor M. I. Pupin, the professor of physics of the institution, continued his experiments in the photographing of invisible objects on the lines laid down by Professor Roentgen, already explained in the HERALD, and obtained very gratifying results. There were many students of the college present while the Professor made his experiments and explained the various phenomena as fast as they developed, and all were most deeply interested in them.
The first photograph taken by the Professor was of the hand of one of the attendants of the college. The picture was excellent and showed the bones and joints of the fingers and of the body of the hand very clearly, the flesh appearing on the plate like a filmy shadow.
Next, the Professor put some nails in an aluminum box, focused the rays from the Crookes tube upon it, and in a short while had a picture of the nails in all their details nearly as faithful to the originals as if they had not been enclosed in a box.

Mr. Tesla, on May 20, 1891, presented to Columbia College the striking results of his very original experiments with alternating currents of great frequency, and in 1892 came to Paris and repeated his experiments before the Society of Physics and the Society of Electricians. Mr. Tesla pointed out a simple method of producing alternating currents of great frequency based upon the properties of induction coils and condensers.
Fig. 1. - Diagram of the arrangement employed for M. Radiguet's Experiments.
A, beginning of the sector; B, circuit breaker; C, bipolar interrupter; D, amperemeter; E, potential reducer; F, vibrator; G, induction coil; H, the D'Arsonval arrangement; K, L, contacts upon the resonator; I, resonator; M, handwheel.
The secondary terminals of a high tension coil are connected with the internal armatures of a Leyden jar which discharges itself disruptively. This disruptive discharge produces alternating currents of great frequency. This process presents a great interest, in that it permits of resuming and completing Tesla's experiments without having recourse to special apparatus that few scientists have at their disposal. by Elihu Thomson
Electrical Engineer
June 24th, 1891

I have been much interested in the account of novel phenomena given under the title " Some Experiments on the Electric Discharge in Vacuum Tubes ," by Prof. J. J. Thomson, and published in your issue of June 10, inasmuch as several months ago I tried the same, or a very similar, experiment to that in which an induced discharge in a closed circuit vacuum receiver was obtained.
Fig. 1. — Electric discharge in vacuum tube.
Briefly, my experiment was performed with a closed ring made of a glass tube about one inch in diameter, the external diameter of the ring being about six inches. This was exhausted to a fairly good vacuum and laid alongside of a single turn of heavily insulated wire, which formed part of the discharge path from the outside of a Leyden jar, arranged to be charged and discharged rapidly by a Toepler-Holtz machine. It was found that at every discharge of the jar there was a discharge in the tube giving a band of light in the vacuous space. The accompanying engraving Fig. 1 shows the arrangement of apparatus as just described.

The following experiments were made to determine the relation between an induction coil and its condenser.
The apparatus used consists of an induction coil and a separate interrupter with a condenser in its base, so arranged with a separate contact that the breaks were made entirely independent of the battery strength passing into the induction coil, a separate cell of battery being used to run the interrupter. The separate interrupter has switches arranged to throw in or out of use the condenser connected to it. The induction coil has an interrupter and condenser of its own, but in making these experiments its interrupter was locked so it could not move, and, of consequence, its condenser was out of use.
I tried the arrangement as described above, and found I obtained from the secondary of the coil fair and vigorous sparks when the interrupter was in use, and the sparks at break of the primary were very small. On throwing out of use the condenser, I found exactly the opposite; the sparks from the secondary were very minute, and the sparks at the break of the primary were largo and bright. BY F. HIMSTEDT IN "WIEDEMANN'S ANNALEN."
The author has succeeded in reproducing most of Tesla's experiments with very simple apparatus. He utilized at first the Lecher method of producing electrical oscillation, but later on used the still more common Leyden jar. The pole of a powerful Rubenkorff coil, 50 centimeters long and 20 centimeters in diameter, and used with five or six accumulator cells, was connected to the inner coatings of two medium-sized Leyden jars insulated from one another by standing on paraffine blocks, and also to a spark micrometer. The outer coatings of the jars were connected together by a copper wire four millimeters thick and 120 centimeters long, bent into U shape. A 16-volt glow lamp put in parallel with this wire was soon brought to incandescence when the spark micrometer was suitably adjusted. When jars 16 centimeters in diameter and 4: centimeters high were used, as many as three lamps could be made to glow — a 65-volt lamp below, a 16-volt lamp in the middle and a 2-volt lamp at the top. If the nipple of such a lamp be filed off it ceases almost entirely to glow. Tesla ascribes this fact to the alteration in the molecular bombardment in the lamp; but the author considers that it is due to the connection of heat by the air admitted.
